blocks.prompt: 2 (i) Let \(f(x) = \sin^{-1}x\). State the domain and range of \(f(x)\) and \(f^{-1}(x)\).
blocks.explanation:
Domain and range of the inverse sine function and of its inverse.
Given \(f(x) = \sin^{-1}x\). Plan: recall that \(\sin^{-1}x\) is the inverse of sine on \(\left[-\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right]\); then swap domain and range.
steps:
Given: \(f(x) = \sin^{-1}x\).
To find: domain and range of \(f\) and of \(f^{-1}\).
Method: \(\sin^{-1}x\) is defined as the inverse of \(\sin x\) restricted to \(\left[-\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right]\), where sine is one-to-one. So \(f^{-1}(x) = \sin x\) on that interval.

Domain of \(f\)
\[D_{f} = [-1, 1]\]
Why: \(\sin^{-1}x\) asks for an angle whose sine is \(x\); a sine is always between \(-1\) and 1.

Range of \(f\)
\[R_{f} = \left[-\tfrac{\pi}{2}, \tfrac{\pi}{2}\right]\]
Why: the answer angle is always taken from the principal interval \(\left[-\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right]\).

Domain and range of \(f^{-1}(x) = \sin x\)
\[D_{f^{-1}} = R_{f} = \left[-\tfrac{\pi}{2}, \tfrac{\pi}{2}\right]\]
\[R_{f^{-1}} = D_{f} = [-1, 1]\]
Why: an inverse interchanges domain and range.

Check:
On \(\left[-\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right]\), \(\sin x\) rises from \(\sin(-\frac{\pi}{2}) = -1\) to \(\sin\frac{\pi}{2} = 1\), so its range is \([-1, 1]\), as found.

blocks.prompt: 2 (ii) Let \(f(x) = \sin^{-1}x\). Sketch the graph of \(f(x)\) and show that it is one-to-one using the horizontal line test.
blocks.explanation:
Sketch the graph, then apply the horizontal line test.
Given \(f(x) = \sin^{-1}x\), \(-1 \le x \le 1\). Plan: plot standard values, join them, then show a line \(y = c\) meets the curve at most once.
steps:
Given: \(f(x) = \sin^{-1}x\), \(x \in [-1, 1]\).
To do: sketch f and show it is one-to-one by the horizontal line test.
Method: use known angles for the table; for the test solve f(x) = c.

Table of values
\[\sin^{-1}(-1) = -\tfrac{\pi}{2} \approx -1.57\]
\[\sin^{-1}\left(-\tfrac{1}{2}\right) = -\tfrac{\pi}{6} \approx -0.52\]
\[\sin^{-1}0 = 0\]
\[\sin^{-1}\tfrac{1}{2} = \tfrac{\pi}{6} \approx 0.52\]
\[\sin^{-1}1 = \tfrac{\pi}{2} \approx 1.57\]
Why: \(\sin\frac{\pi}{6} = \frac{1}{2}\) and \(\sin\frac{\pi}{2} = 1\); sine is odd, so the negative values follow.

Sketch
Join the points by a smooth curve from \(\left(-1, -\frac{\pi}{2}\right)\) to \(\left(1, \frac{\pi}{2}\right)\). The graph has two end points (closed dots) and rises all the way.
Why: the domain is the closed interval [−1, 1], so the graph stops at both ends.

Horizontal line test with \(y = c\)
\[\sin^{-1}x = c,\quad -\tfrac{\pi}{2} \le c \le \tfrac{\pi}{2}\]
\[x = \sin c\]
Why: for each such \(c\) there is exactly one \(x = \sin c\). If \(c\) is outside \(\left[-\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right]\), the line does not meet the graph at all. So no line meets it more than once.

Check:
The line \(y = 0.5\) meets the curve only near \(x = \sin 0.5 \approx 0.48\), and \(y = 1.2\) only near \(x = \sin 1.2 \approx 0.93\); \(y = -1\) only at \(x = \sin(-1) \approx -0.84\).
blocks.final_answer: The graph of \(y = \sin^{-1}x\) is a rising curve from \(\left(-1, -\frac{\pi}{2}\right)\) to \(\left(1, \frac{\pi}{2}\right)\); every horizontal line meets it at most once, so \(f\) is one-to-one.

answer_figure.caption: y = sin⁻¹x on [−1, 1]: each horizontal line meets it at most once

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The answer key has no entry for Question 2 (ii). The graph of \(f(x) = \sin^{-1}x\) and the horizontal line test are given together under (iii).

blocks.prompt: 2 (iii) Let \(f(x) = \sin^{-1}x\). Draw the graph of \(f^{-1}(x)\) and verify that it is the reflection of \(f(x)\) in the line \(y = x\).
blocks.explanation:
Draw the inverse and compare it with f.
Given \(f(x) = \sin^{-1}x\), so \(f^{-1}(x) = \sin x\), \(-\frac{\pi}{2} \le x \le \frac{\pi}{2}\). Plan: swap the coordinates of the points of part (ii), draw \(\sin x\) through them, and check the mirror property.
steps:
Given: \(f(x) = \sin^{-1}x\), \(f^{-1}(x) = \sin x\), \(x \in \left[-\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right]\).
To verify: the graph of \(f^{-1}\) is the reflection of the graph of \(f\) in \(y = x\).
Method: \((a, b)\) on \(f\) gives \((b, a)\) on \(f^{-1}\); \((b, a)\) is the mirror image of \((a, b)\) in \(y = x\).

Points of the inverse
\[\left(-1, -\tfrac{\pi}{2}\right) \to \left(-\tfrac{\pi}{2}, -1\right)\]
\[\left(-\tfrac{1}{2}, -\tfrac{\pi}{6}\right) \to \left(-\tfrac{\pi}{6}, -\tfrac{1}{2}\right)\]
\[(0, 0) \to (0, 0)\]
\[\left(\tfrac{1}{2}, \tfrac{\pi}{6}\right) \to \left(\tfrac{\pi}{6}, \tfrac{1}{2}\right)\]
\[\left(1, \tfrac{\pi}{2}\right) \to \left(\tfrac{\pi}{2}, 1\right)\]
Why: these are exactly the points of \(y = \sin x\): for example \(\sin\frac{\pi}{6} = \frac{1}{2}\).

Mirror property
\[\text{slope} = \dfrac{a - b}{b - a} = -1\]
Each joining segment is perpendicular to \(y = x\) and its midpoint \(\left(\frac{a+b}{2}, \frac{a+b}{2}\right)\) lies on \(y = x\).
Why: so \(y = x\) is the perpendicular bisector of every pair: the two graphs are reflections.

Compare the shapes
Both curves pass through the origin. For \(x > 0\) the curve \(\sin^{-1}x\) lies above \(y = x\) and \(\sin x\) lies below it by the same distance; for \(x < 0\) it is the other way round.
Why: reflection in y = x swaps the sides of the line.

Check:
End points: \(f\) ends at \(\left(1, \frac{\pi}{2}\right) \approx (1, 1.57)\) and \(f^{-1}\) at \(\left(\frac{\pi}{2}, 1\right) \approx (1.57, 1)\): swapped coordinates, as expected.
blocks.final_answer: \(f^{-1}(x) = \sin x\), \(-\frac{\pi}{2} \le x \le \frac{\pi}{2}\): the sine curve from \(\left(-\frac{\pi}{2}, -1\right)\) through \((0, 0)\) to \(\left(\frac{\pi}{2}, 1\right)\). It is the reflection of \(y = \sin^{-1}x\) in the line \(y = x\).

answer_figure.alt: The curves y = inverse sine of x (from (-1, -pi/2) to (1, pi/2)) and y = sin x for x from -pi/2 to pi/2 (from (-pi/2, -1) to (pi/2, 1)) with the line y = x; dashed segments join (1, pi/2) to (pi/2, 1) and (-1, -pi/2) to (-pi/2, -1).
answer_figure.caption: y = sin⁻¹x and y = sin x, −π/2 ≤ x ≤ π/2, are mirror images in y = x
